beginner: Gas prices just spiked 21% in two weeks, the worst jump since 1967, sending overall inflation to 3.3% in March. War disruptions in the Middle East are making energy expensive again.
A ceasefire between the US and Iran just started, but nobody knows if it will hold. Energy markets are now waiting to see if this actually sticks or falls apart.
The Fed has room to cut rates later this year if inflation cools down, but the war risk means that plan could change fast depending on what happens with the ceasefire.
moderate: Annual inflation jumped 0.9 points to 3.3% in March, almost entirely from energy (12.5% annual, gasoline 18.9%), reversing three months of cooling that had taken inflation down from 2.41% in February. This is the highest print since May 2024 and breaks the disinflationary trend.

The Iran war premium alone accounts for the entire monthly surge, with gas prices up 21.2% month-over-month. Without the energy shock, core inflation likely stayed flat or improved, so this is a geopolitical shock, not a monetary one.

A two-week ceasefire agreement removes some tail risk to oil supply, but markets are pricing in significant uncertainty about whether it holds. Rate cuts that looked likely for mid-2026 are now contingent on energy stability, not just core inflation metrics.
expert: March CPI printed 3.3%, a 90 basis point jump from 2.41% in February, driven entirely by energy components (gasoline up 18.9% annually, 21.2% monthly). The war with Iran created a clear supply shock; without it, the disinflationary narrative held intact.

The gasoline spike is the largest monthly move since 1967, reflecting genuine supply constraints, not demand pull. Core inflation mechanics remain benign, but the energy tail risk is now material enough to keep the Fed on hold despite 2.2% full-year growth expectations.

Watch the ceasefire duration and NYMEX crude pathways. If the two-week agreement extends and crude retreats toward $70-75 per barrel, April CPI should normalize sharply downward, allowing rate cuts to resume. If tensions reignite, inflation stays above 3% through mid-year despite weak underlying demand.

beginner: Canadian inflation is creeping up from trade fights with the US, but the central bank expects tariff effects to fade by the end of 2026, bringing inflation down by 0.3 to 0.4 percentage points.

The Bank of Canada is caught between two pressures: tariffs pushing prices higher right now, but the delayed hit from those tariffs could slow down the rate cuts they were planning to make early in 2026.

If trade tensions cool down, Canada's inflation drops back toward 2% and the central bank can cut rates more aggressively. But tariff delays mean they have to move cautiously until the picture clears up.
moderate: Canada's core inflation is holding above the 2% target due to tariff pass-through, but consensus expects those effects to fade through the year, allowing a 0.3 to 0.4 point decline by year-end. The delayed timing of tariff absorption is what matters: it's slowing rate cuts right now even though the underlying disinflationary trend is real.

The Bank of Canada faces a timing mismatch between policy needs and tariff dynamics. Tariffs pushed up input costs in Q1 2026, but their full retail pass-through lags by months, creating uncertainty about when to accelerate cuts. This is why rate cut pace is slowing in the first half despite an expected 1.7% growth forecast.

Monitor the USD/CAD cross and US trade policy signals. If the US eases tariffs or grandfathers Canadian products, the tariff premium drops fast and the BoC can cut more aggressively by Q3. If tariffs harden, inflation stays sticky and the central bank stays on pause longer than growth needs.
expert: Core inflation is being artificially elevated by tariff pass-through, but consensus sees a 30-40 basis point decline through 2026 as those effects roll off. The policy rate is already at 2.25% (Feb 2026), and the delayed tariff absorption is why rate cuts are on hold in H1 despite 1.7% growth and a 6.74% unemployment rate (Jan 2026).

The timing of tariff pass-through is critical to the BoC's reaction function. Retail prices will continue to absorb input tariffs through Q2-Q3, keeping near-term inflation sticky even as the underlying trend weakens. This explains the cautious forward guidance despite weak growth.

If US tariff policy reverses or moderates by May, tariff expectations collapse and the BoC cuts 50-75 basis points in H2 2026. If tariffs persist or escalate, core inflation remains elevated above 2.5% through year-end and the central bank remains restricted to 25 basis point increments, depressing asset prices and widening the output gap.

beginner: The UK ran a huge budget deficit last year (5.4% of GDP) while public debt is near 100% of GDP, leaving the government with less room to borrow or spend during downturns.

Inflation is slowly cooling as tariffs and administered price hikes work through the system, heading toward 2% by the end of 2026. The pound just jumped 1% on the Iran ceasefire news, which helps the Bank of England's inflation story.
Growth is expected to stay weak at 1.5% this year, so the Bank of England will probably keep rates steady around 3.75% to manage the debt burden without strangling an already fragile economy.
moderate: The UK's 5.4% budget deficit for 2025 is the second-largest of the forecast period and combined with 100% public debt creates structural fiscal pressure. This limits the government's ability to respond to growth shocks and constrains monetary policy flexibility, forcing the central bank to maintain higher rates longer than growth alone would justify.

Core inflation is expected to decline 1 percentage point (from ~3% now to 2% by year-end) as tariff pass-through and administered price impacts fade. The pound gained 1% after the US-Iran ceasefire announcement, which eases imported inflation pressures and supports disinflationary momentum.

The Bank of England's rate path is constrained by fiscal sustainability, not demand. Growth at 1.5% suggests room for cuts, but the debt situation (100% of GDP) means the central bank cannot ease aggressively without validating higher long-term gilt yields and triggering fiscal stress. Watch gilt spreads for signs of fiscal fragility.
expert: The UK's 5.4% deficit for 2025 combined with 100% of GDP public debt creates a fiscal dominance constraint on monetary policy. The central bank sits at 3.75% (Feb 2026) despite 1.5% growth expectations and 5.2% unemployment (Nov 2025), suggesting rates remain restrictive due to debt concerns, not inflation control.

Core inflation is tracking toward the lower end of the disinflationary path (currently 3.24% in Feb 2026, expected to reach 2% by year-end), driven by tariff pass-through completion and administered price base effects. The 1% GBP rally on the Iran ceasefire reduces import cost pressures further.

The key forward risk is gilt yields. If international investors reprrice UK sovereign risk due to debt concerns, long-term rates rise sharply regardless of BoE policy, creating a tightening without the central bank needing to act. Conversely, if fiscal consolidation credibly begins in 2027, the BoE gains room to cut to 2.75-3% by year-end, supporting the 1.5% growth forecast.

beginner: Japanese consumers just got spooked. Confidence collapsed from 39.7 to 33.3, the worst drop in years, even though companies are investing heavily in new machines and equipment.

This split is strange: households are fearful and pulling back on spending, but factories are ordering machines at a 28% pace, suggesting companies believe growth is coming. Japan's economy is caught between consumer panic and corporate optimism.

Inflation has been slightly above the Bank of Japan's 2% target, but it is expected to fall below 2% by late 2026 as the year progresses. The central bank is unlikely to raise rates again soon given this consumer weakness.
moderate: Household confidence plunged to 33.3 from 39.7 (consensus 38.3), signaling severe consumer retrenchment that contradicts the strong 28.1% surge in machine tool orders (up from 24.2% year-over-year). This divergence suggests companies are betting on export demand and future productivity gains, but households are not confident enough to spend today.

Current inflation at 1.26% (Feb 2026) sits below the BoJ's 2% target despite the global cost-push environment, reflecting weak domestic demand transmission. The expected drift below 2% by late 2026 means the disinflationary pressure from low consumer confidence is winning out over external price pressures.

The BoJ's 0.75% policy rate (Feb 2026) is appropriate for this split: too tight to support consumer demand, too loose to justify raising into capex momentum. Watch export orders next. If they continue to drive machine tool orders higher but household confidence stays in the low 30s, the BoJ faces a demand composition problem: strong external demand but domestic demand destruction.
expert: Household confidence collapsed to 33.3 (from 39.7), the worst print in this cycle, while machine tool orders surged 28.1% year-over-year (from 24.2%), creating a stark demand bifurcation. Consumers are pulling back on spending despite nominal wage growth; companies are doubling down on capex, betting on export recovery.

CPI printed 1.26% in February 2026, below the BoJ's 2% target and tracking toward sub-2% by late 2026 despite the weak yen (which should import inflation). The household confidence collapse is transmitting into demand destruction faster than external price shocks are lifting inflation, signaling deflationary dynamics at work.

The BoJ's easing bias faces a transmission problem. Machine tool orders suggest capex demand remains intact at the 2% policy rate, but consumer confidence at 33.3 indicates households are not participating in the recovery. If export momentum falters in Q2-Q3 2026, the capex cycle may reverse sharply, creating a tail risk to growth forecasts (0.8% full-year) and forcing the BoJ back to accommodation despite already loose policy.

beginner: Germany's factories are slowing down and the economy is struggling, but the government is about to spend big money on defense and infrastructure which should help later this year.
Inflation cooled to 1.9% in February, meaning prices aren't rising much right now, so the central bank has room to cut rates if things get worse.
Germany is stuck in a demographic trap where fewer young people are entering the workforce, making it harder to grow the economy even with government support.
moderate: Industrial production missed forecasts recently, signaling that the manufacturing-export engine that normally powers German growth has stalled, a sharper turn than Italy's downturn but both tied to weak demand across Europe.

At 1.9% CPI in February, Germany is running below the 2.2% full-year forecast, giving policymakers headroom to ease policy if the construction and defense stimulus doesn't gain traction quickly enough.

Government spending on defense and infrastructure should lift growth in late 2026 and into 2027, but the timing is uncertain and euro area growth remains capped at 1.1% as France consolidates its budget.
expert: Industrial production collapsed relative to expectations while CPI printed 1.9% in February, below consensus, leaving the ECB room to cut if Q2 momentum falters and pushing rate expectations lower than the 2.5% full-year forecast.

Fiscal support targeting defense and infrastructure spending is frontloaded for 2026-2027, but deployment lags outside those sectors, creating a growth schedule risk if multipliers disappoint or geopolitical demand shifts.

With unemployment at 3.6% and a 4.5% current account surplus, Germany has the external and labor market capacity to absorb stimulus, but demographic headwinds and weak industrial capex signal underlying demand destruction that spending alone may not reverse.

beginner: France's job market is weak at 7.7% unemployment and the government is cutting spending to shrink the budget deficit, which means the economy will struggle to grow even though French airplane makers are doing well.
Inflation collapsed to 0.9% in February, the lowest in Europe, showing French consumers and businesses aren't spending much right now.
Political chaos in parliament is blocking budget reform, making it hard for the government to fix its massive deficit and leaving France vulnerable if the economy weakens further.
moderate: At 0.9% CPI in February, France is running nearly a full percentage point below the 2% forecast and is the softest reading in the eurozone, reflecting a labor market frozen at 7.7% unemployment and consumers rationing spending before fiscal cuts kick in.
Exporters in aerospace and defense are benefiting from German government orders, but that demand boost is too narrow to offset slowing domestic consumption and the fiscal tightening cycle ahead.

The political divided legislature is blocking budget revisions meant to tackle a deficit forecast at 4.8% of GDP, the highest in the eurozone ex-Greece, trapping the government between austerity demands and growth needs.
expert: CPI fell to 0.9% in February, 110 basis points below the full-year 2% forecast, signaling demand destruction that will persist as the government implements fiscal consolidation and unemployment stays stuck above 7.5%.

Aerospace and defense orders are flowing but remain a narrow wedge, while broader industrial activity is softening in sync with German weakness, indicating the German fiscal impulse is insufficient to pull France's export base when domestic demand is this fragile.

With the deficit at 4.8% and a divided legislature blocking reform, fiscal space is contracting while growth momentum is retreating, creating policy rigidity at precisely the moment countercyclical support would help most.

beginner: Italy's factories are slowing down like Germany and France, but not as badly, which suggests the broader European downturn is real but Italy is holding up slightly better.
Inflation is on track to hit the 2% target in 2026, meaning prices will stabilize and the central bank has less pressure to keep rates high.
Italy's public debt is massive at over 135% of GDP, the second-worst in Europe, so even small economic stumbles could make borrowing costs jump and force more painful budget cuts.
moderate: Italy's industrial downturn is milder than Germany's but still real, and at 1.51% CPI in February the country is tracking toward the 2% full-year target, providing some breathing room before the summer inflation season.

Unemployment at 5.6% is the lowest among the three large eurozone countries, giving Italy's labor market an edge, but the debt burden at 135% of GDP means fiscal space to respond to shocks is near zero.

Unlike Germany's front-loaded fiscal stimulus or France's consolidation squeeze, Italy's deficit is forecast at 3.2% of GDP, a middle ground that reflects sustained fiscal discipline without room for error if growth disappoints.
expert: Industrial production is cooling in line with the eurozone, CPI at 1.51% in February is tracking well toward the 2% full-year target, and unemployment at 5.6% is the region's lowest, creating a relatively stable demand backdrop for 2026.

The deficit at 3.2% of GDP is the lowest among the big three and reflects years of attempted debt reduction, but the stock of debt at 135% and high borrowing costs leave zero room for policy error if growth slips below forecast.

With moderate growth at 1% expected and deficit consolidation ongoing, Italy has little fiscal lever if the eurozone slowdown deepens, making it structurally dependent on ECB rate cuts to avoid a refinancing squeeze on its debt service burden.

beginner: China's prices are barely rising (CPI at 1.0% in March when it should be 1.2%), and monthly prices actually fell, which means the economy is so weak that deflation is a real risk right now.
China is losing cash reserves, with $86 billion in foreign exchange leaving the country recently, a sign that capital flight and economic uncertainty are starting to accelerate.

Unlike every other major economy, China is the only one facing deflation risk during the Iran war, showing that domestic demand has collapsed despite official factory data looking okay on the surface.
moderate: CPI slowed to 1.0% year-on-year in March with the monthly reading down 0.7%, both weaker than expected, and China alone among major economies faces persistent deflation risk as domestic demand refuses to respond to policy stimulus.

FX reserves dropped $86 billion recently, signaling that capital is fleeing despite official PMI strength, a divergence that reveals the PMI rebound is narrow (state-owned factory activity) while private demand and confidence remain broken.

China's 4.7% growth forecast assumes stimulus will eventually ignite consumption, but the deflation signal and capital outflow suggest that assumption is at risk, particularly if geopolitical shocks or US policy tighten financial conditions further.
expert: March CPI printed 1.0% year-on-year versus consensus 1.2% with monthly -0.7% versus -0.2% expected, and China is the sole major economy where deflation risk persists, indicating that stimulus has failed to reignite the demand anchor needed for inflation reflation.

FX reserves dropped $86 billion amid economic pressure, a flow signal that contradicts the official PMI rebound above 50, exposing the composition risk: state capacity is recovering but private consumption, capex, and confidence remain severely impaired.

The 4.7% full-year growth forecast assumes demand stabilization, but the deflation channel and capital outflow trajectory suggest China's policy transmission is broken and additional stimulus may simply flow to reserve accumulation rather than final demand, creating a 2026 growth miss risk.

beginner: India's economy grew 8% in the first half of 2026, much stronger than most countries, because businesses rushed to sell goods before US tariffs hit. That's real momentum underneath the noise.

Inflation dropped to just 1.33% in December, which means the central bank has room to cut interest rates and help businesses borrow more cheaply. The policy rate sits at 5.25%, down from 6% forecasted.
The tariff-driven export surge won't last forever. Once US trade barriers fully kick in, South Asian growth will slow from the current 10.8% pace to just 6.2% next year, a dramatic deceleration.
moderate: India's 8% first-half growth reflects front-loaded exports as firms race to beat US tariffs, creating a temporary sugar high. This compares sharply to South Asia's typical 6% trend and explains why full-year forecasts show 10.8% despite expected slowdown.

Inflation at 1.33% is remarkably low for an emerging market and sits well below the 4.2% annual forecast, giving the Reserve Bank of India genuine flexibility to ease policy if growth falters. The 5.25% policy rate already reflects this dovish positioning.

The tariff-driven export pull-forward will reverse sharply once trade barriers fully settle, and South Asia is projected to decelerate to 6.2% growth in 2026, a 460 basis point drop from the artificially elevated current pace.
expert: Real GDP expanded 8% year-over-year in H1 2026 on tariff-driven export front-loading, but this masks a structural slowdown. South Asian growth decelerates from current 10.8% to 6.2% in 2026 as the tariff arbitrage window closes.

CPI at 1.33% in December sits 280 basis points below the 4.2% full-year forecast, signaling either demand weakness or base effects, while the policy rate at 5.25% is 75 basis points below the 6% expected midpoint, indicating the RBI has already priced in a normalization cycle.

Watch for the timing of the tariff-driven export reversal and whether domestic investment and consumption can fill the void. If not, the central bank faces a dilemma: cut further into weak demand or hold to manage currency pressures from the 1.2% current account deficit.

beginner: South Africa just lost $3.3 billion in foreign exchange reserves, a sign investors are pulling money out of the country. Alongside China doing the same, this raises questions about emerging market stability.

Unemployment sits at a crushing 31.88%, nearly the worst in the world, while inflation at 2.96% is actually well-behaved. The central bank cannot cut rates to help workers because the economy needs the currency to stay strong.

Regional growth is expected to improve to 4.3% in 2026 as other African countries invest and reform, but South Africa itself is only forecast to grow 1.5%, leaving the country increasingly behind its neighbors.
moderate: South Africa's FX reserves dropped $3.3 billion to $77.76 billion, paralleling China's significant drawdown, suggesting a coordinated emerging market de-risking. Net reserves fell to $73.187 billion, a warning signal that external buffers are shrinking.

Inflation at 2.96% in February is remarkably low and anchored well, yet unemployment sits at 31.88%, the third worst globally. The policy rate at 6.75% cannot move lower despite the inflation strength because currency stability depends on rate support.

Sub-Saharan Africa overall is projected to accelerate to 4.3% in 2026 on investment and reform momentum, but South Africa's 1.5% growth forecast suggests the country is losing regional competitiveness and will lag peers.
expert: FX reserves declined $3.3 billion to $77.76 billion (net reserves $73.187 billion) in recent months, paralleling China's reserve drawdown and signaling coordinated capital outflows from emerging markets. The reserve depletion rate matters for rand stability given the 1.4% current account deficit.

CPI at 2.96% in February sits 54 basis points below the 3.5% full-year forecast, yet the policy rate at 6.75% is 50 basis points above the 6.25% midpoint forecast, reflecting the SARB's conviction that external stability trumps domestic demand. Unemployment at 31.88% is the binding constraint.

Watch reserve adequacy metrics closely: at current drawdown rates, the SARB's external buffer erodes faster than growth can rebuild it. The policy rate cannot normalize lower without triggering further capital flight, a structural trap that only growth can break.

beginner: Brazil might slap tariffs on steel even though it depends on Chinese money flowing in, a risky move that could provoke retaliation and scare off investors. This is desperation policy, not sound economics.

The central bank is cutting interest rates by 250 basis points in 2026, bringing them down from 15% toward normal levels. This is a big bet that inflation is under control, because hiking back up would destroy the economy.
Latin America is barely growing (2.3% forecast), and Brazil is only expected to grow 1.7%, which means the tariff fight won't help much. The real problem is weak domestic demand, not trade barriers.
moderate: Brazil is considering sector-specific tariffs on steel despite heavy reliance on Chinese investment, a gambit that prioritizes short-term manufacturing over long-term capital inflows. This reflects political pressure to show action amid trade tensions.

The central bank is expected to cut 250 basis points in 2026, moving from an extraordinary 15% toward a normalized 12%. CPI at 3.81% in February gives room for cuts, but the pace is aggressive and assumes no external shocks.

Latin America is projected to grow just 2.3% in 2026 amid trade tensions and weak domestic demand, with Brazil at only 1.7%, so tariffs alone won't drive recovery. The real drag is sluggish consumption and investment, which rate cuts are meant to unlock.
expert: Brazil is contemplating sector-specific steel tariffs despite dependency on Chinese investment, a policy that signals escalating trade friction tolerance and shifts downside risk to FDI flows. The move matters more symbolically than economically given Brazil's 2.6% current account deficit.

The central bank is anchored on 250 basis points of cuts in 2026, bringing the policy rate from 15% toward the 12% full-year forecast, while CPI at 3.81% in February is 39 basis points below the 4.2% midpoint. This suggests the disinflation story is holding, but the easing pace assumes external stability.

Watch the policy rate path as a proxy for confidence in capital inflows. If tariff escalation spooks investors and triggers currency depreciation, the central bank will pause cuts mid-cycle, forcing a choice between supporting growth or defending the real. Latin America's 2.3% growth forecast leaves no margin for error.

beginner: Russia's war in Ukraine keeps grinding on, and economists find that prolonged conflicts destroy more wealth than even financial crises do. The longer this lasts, the worse the economic fallout across Europe and for Russia itself.

Inflation in Russia hit 6.01% in January and stays elevated, while unemployment is incredibly low at 2.15%. This means the economy is overheating from war spending, not from healthy demand. The central bank jacked rates to 15.5% to try to cool things down.

Europe got hit hard by the invasion, with countries forced to spend massively on energy and defense right when their economies were already weak. The war created a macro catastrophe that high interest rates alone cannot fix.
moderate: Russia's invasion of Ukraine continues to generate persistent output losses that exceed financial crises, with spillovers hitting regional economies through energy shocks and uncertainty. The conflict duration is now the key macro variable, not fiscal or monetary policy.

CPI at 6.01% in January sits 131 basis points above the 4.7% full-year forecast, while unemployment sits at 2.15%, well below the 2.5% forecast. The policy rate at 15.5% is 300 basis points above the 12.5% midpoint, signaling aggressive tightening to combat war-driven demand and supply shocks.

The EU energy crisis triggered by the invasion forced governments into countercyclical spending during economic contraction, creating acute macroeconomic trade-offs that monetary policy cannot resolve. The conflict's persistence is the binding constraint on European recovery, not rate moves.
expert: Armed conflict generates output losses that persist well beyond financial crises, with Russia's invasion creating sustained regional spillovers through energy supply disruption and capital flight. The conflict's duration, not its end date, is the dominant downside risk to Europe's 2026 growth trajectory.

CPI at 6.01% in January sits 131 basis points above the 4.7% forecast midpoint, while the policy rate at 15.5% is 300 basis points above the 12.5% full-year expectation. Unemployment at 2.15% shows the Russian economy is war-mobilized and overheated, not normalizing.

Watch whether European governments attempt fiscal normalization in 2026 after energy crisis spending. If they consolidate while the conflict persists, growth slows further. If they don't, inflation and fiscal deficits remain elevated. The war breaks the normal macro framework.
